about: The words of the chain wine_fleet (Data/encounters/chain_wine_fleet_793.json; Design/content/chains/wine_fleet.md): the wine fleet to the fair of Saint-Denis. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: Radbern, his daughter Aldburg, Leofstan of Hamwic, Brother Waldric the cellarer and Ursio the cooper are invented ordinary people; Abbot Fardulf is historical (abbot 793 to 806); the reeve at Lundenwic is the spine's Wighelm. Nothing is quoted from any text: the judgment of 753 and the king's letter of 796 are given in our own plain words. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: A second keel

Radbern has gone up the Seine to the fair of Saint-Denis every October for twenty years, with a ship and a boat. This summer the boat is firewood. He stands on the dam and looks at yours for a long time before he speaks.
Twenty Octobers I have drunk the saint's health in the saint's own wine. I would like to make it twenty-one.
My ship carries the wine. But the river above Rotomagus is all bends and shoals, and a ship wants a small boat ahead of her that can turn. Yours can turn.
And the kings have made it up. A merchant is to have his old protection again on both sides of the water. The English will be on the Seine this year with wool, so cloth must be there first.
Cloth up, wine down. Carry my best bolts going and my best casks coming, and take a share. We leave after Michaelmas and we are home by Martinmas, if God and the bungs hold.
I cut the tally, not him. He has never brought home the same number he took out. He says casks leak.
Join hands: sail as his second keel for a share
Sail in his company, but for your own purse
Not this year. Ask him what cloth fetches at the fair

Aldburg splits a hazel stick down its length and gives you the half with your notches. Four bolts of his best cloth go under your thwarts. You are to be at Rotomagus for the flood tides after Michaelmas, and at the saint's strand for his Mass.
He shrugs. A man may sail beside another man. He pays you twenty pennies to carry two bolts and tells you the day: the saint's strand, for Saint Denis's Mass, nine days into October.

He tells you anyway, since it costs him nothing: the monks and the vine-dressers pay a fifth over the Dorestat price for good Frisian cloth while the fair lasts, because every man there has wine and none of them has a cloak. He will ask you again next summer.
The tide and the toll

Under the south wall of Rotomagus the boats for the fair lie in a row, waiting for the flood to carry them up. Frisians, men of Hamwic, a boat of monks. The king's toll man works along the row with a tally and a boy.
Cloth going up, wine coming down. Every autumn the same, and every autumn somebody tells me his bolts are a gift for his sister. The king takes his part of what goes up to be sold.
That boat pays nothing. Saint Germain's men, with the king's writing. If you had a saint you could try it. You have a sister.
Leofstan, of Hamwic. Wool, mostly. We were shut out of here for six years while two kings argued about a wedding. I mean to make up all six this month.
Half this row will be pilgrims when he reaches them. A staff, a bundle, a sad face. The king has written that true pilgrims go free and false ones pay. He did not write how to tell.
From here to the saint the river goes five days to cover two. Sit a tide with me and I will tell you where it lies to you.
Show the cloth and pay the king's toll
Put the bolts under a pilgrim's bundle and say you are bound for the saint
Lie over a tide and have the river man tell you the loops
Six pennies. He notches his tally and yours, and says that a man who shows his cloth going up will find the toll lighter coming down.
He looks at the bundle, at your face, and at the long row still ahead of him. He blesses your journey without warmth and moves on. The Englishman, two boats down, has been a pilgrim since noon.
The boy lifts the bundle with one finger. Underneath is a great deal of cloth for a penitent. The toll man takes twice the toll, twelve pennies, and says the saint will be told.

You lose the flood and gain the river. He names every loop, the island where the stream splits, the bank that was not there last year, and the abbey you will see on your left hand a day before you see the city. By the time he has finished, the toll man has gone up the row and not come back.
Saint Denis's Mass

The strand below the abbey is boats from the willows to the island. Bells, smoke, carts of casks coming down from the vineyards. The abbey's man takes the toll at the water. Behind him a man in the count's colours is counting heads.
There. The saint's church, the saint's strand, the saint's toll man. For a month everything here is the saint's, down to the mud. It saves argument.
They say the church has a hundred windows and one. A man of ours began to count them once. He stopped when he thought of the price of the glass.
From the saint's Mass until the market ends, every toll in this country is Saint Denis's: boats, landing, carts, pack beasts, wheels, bridges, gates. You pay me, and you pay once.
And four pennies a head to the count, for every free man who comes to trade. It was paid in his grandfather's day. Four men: sixteen pennies.
A slave pays five. He must first swear that he is a slave. I have never understood why more men do not think of it, and then I remember the penny.
My father paid that. Then the merchants stopped coming, the monks went to King Pippin, and the king struck it down. Before I was born. This one is hoping we are all too young to know.
Pay the sixteen pennies for your four heads
Say aloud, before the abbey's man, that King Pippin struck this tax down
Pay nobody yet. Walk up to the abbey gate and ask whose toll it is
Sixteen pennies. The count's man is pleasant about it. The abbey's toll man watches the silver go into the wrong purse and writes nothing down, which with him is a way of remembering.

You say it loudly enough for the next six boats. The abbey's man says that he has seen the writing, with the old king's mark, and that it is kept in a chest not two hundred paces from here. The count's man remembers business in the city. The abbey halves your toll for the month.
You say it, but you say the wrong king. The count's man corrects you kindly, takes eight pennies as a friend, and goes on down the strand. The abbey's man was talking to a carter and heard nothing.

It costs you the first day of the fair. The porter sends for the cellarer, the cellarer listens with his head on one side, and says the toll is the saint's and nobody else's, and that he will be glad to know which of the count's men thinks otherwise. He asks your name, and your boat's.
The cellarer's wine

The cloth is sold, and your part of it is in your purse. In the abbey's long storehouse Brother Waldric, the cellarer, walks you between three rows of casks. Radbern has bought for his ship already. The casks for your boat he leaves to you.
This row is the wine of this year, pressed at Saint Remigius's Mass. Cheap. That row is last year's, and has stopped arguing with itself. Dear. The third row is the lord abbot's and is not for sale.
Listen. The new wine is still working. Put your ear there. Leave its bung loose until Martinmas or it will open the cask for you, between two staves, at night.
And any wine: keep the cask full and keep it still. An empty hand's breadth under the bung is where vinegar begins. More wine is spoiled by rowing than by years.
You are the one who spoke about the saint's toll. The lord abbot heard. There are two casks of his own that want carrying north, to be paid for when they are sold. He does not offer that to pilgrims.
Three of the cheap or two of the dear. I have lost money both ways. Choose, and then you cannot blame me.
A book-bishop of the English made a riddle on this very thing. Take it with you. If you cannot answer it by the time you are home, ask the cask.
The wine of this year: cheap, three casks, still working
Last year's wine: dear, two casks, settled
The abbot's own casks, under the abbey's mark, on trust
Three casks of the year's wine go down to the strand on a cart. They tick and whisper in the boat like something asleep. The bungs are loose, and stay loose until you decide otherwise.
Two casks of last year's wine, quiet as stones. The cellarer drives the bungs himself and says they may stay driven.

Two casks with the abbey's mark burned into the head. Old wine, settled, better than anything on the strand. Brother Waldric writes your name on a strip of parchment and puts it where he will find it again.
The partner's casks

Twelve days into the fair Radbern does not come down to the strand. He is in the hospice at the abbey gate, on straw, with a fever. His steersman has the ship. His tally and his best casks are in your boat.
It comes with the fair every year. Too many men, one well. Some are up in a week. Some we carry across the yard.
The stick. Take the stick. Aldburg has the other half. The casks under your thwarts are the best I bought. Put them on her floor. Not on the dam. On her floor.
We joined hands. I do not have to say the rest.
You sail for your own purse. I knew that when I put my casks in your boat. I am asking all the same.

A word, away from the door. Sick men's wine is hard to carry and easy to quarrel over. I will give two hundred and forty pennies for his casks today, on this strand. His daughter gets silver, which does not leak.
If you mean to wait for him, know what you are waiting into. After Martinmas the wind goes round to the north-east and the river smokes in the mornings.
Take his tally and his casks, and sail for Dorestat while the weather holds
Stay by him until the fever turns, and sail late
Sell his casks to the Englishman here for ready silver

You put the stick inside your shirt. He nods, and turns his face to the wall to save his strength. The brother says they will do what is done. You sail on the morning stream with the weather still soft.

Nine nights. You fetch water, since the brothers have forty others, and one of them teaches you the words they say over the cup, to pass the time. On the tenth morning Radbern asks what day it is and whether the bungs are loose. You sail after Martinmas, late, into a north-east wind.

Two hundred and forty pennies, counted twice on a cask head. The Englishman's men roll the casks along the strand. The tally stick is still inside your shirt, and the silver is his daughter's until you stand in her house and say otherwise.
The cooper under the wall
At Rotomagus a cooper works along the boats under the wall with a mallet in one hand and a jug in the other. He raps each of your casks with his knuckle and listens, like a man at a door.
Hear that? That one says yes. This one says maybe. A cask should sound like a full man, not a hungry one. You have lost a hand's breadth since the saint.
And this is this year's. Still talking. Whatever you do at sea, do not hammer that bung home because it frightens you. It is meant to frighten you.
Settled wine. Good. Fill it, drive the bung, and then leave it alone. It has finished with the world. Let it be.
Twelve pennies, I fill and hoop the lot. Or thirty for the winter and I come with you. I have made casks for the sea all my life and never seen where they go.
Have him fill the casks to the bung and drive the hoops
Hire him for the winter: he wants to see the sea
Keep your pennies. Ask him what the English boats said of the price
He fills each cask from his jug until it wets the bung, and drives the willow hoops down a finger with the mallet. Rapped again, they all say yes.

Ursio comes aboard with his mallet, his jug and a bag of hoops, fills every cask before he will sit down, and is sick over the side before the city is out of sight. He goes on rapping the casks between times.

He does not hold it against you. The Hamwic boats came in on yesterday's flood, he says, and their men were saying that over the sea wine pays a fifth more than it did, and will until Christmas, since the lords there have six dry years to wash out.
Frost on the bung

In the night the wind goes north-east and hard. By morning there is ice on the sheets and a white rim on the gunwale. The casks work against their chocks with every sea, and one of them weeps at the bung.
She is weeping. There. I can stop it with the mallet, or we can slow down and coddle them. Or we run and trust the chocks.
It is the new wine. The monk said loose until Martinmas. He was standing on a stone floor when he said it.
It is the settled wine. The monk said a driven bung would do it no harm. Shaking would.
We are a fortnight behind every other boat. I say that as a fact, not a complaint.
Shorten sail, bed the casks in the cloaks and ease the bungs
Carry all sail and get in before the frost does
Drive every bung home with the mallet and hold your course
A slow, cold day. The men give up their cloaks to the casks and say what they think of wine. The weeping stops. Nothing moves under the thwarts but the boat.
She carries it. The chocks hold, the coast goes by, and you are inside before the frost has made up its mind. The men are pleased with themselves and say so.

A sea comes over the quarter and a chock goes. For half a watch the casks roll a hand's breadth each way before they are wedged again. One man has a crushed foot. Whatever had settled in the wine is all through it now.
The mallet stops the weeping at once. The casks are tight as drums and silent. Whether that silence is good news depends on what is inside them.
The first cup

The first cask is broached on the quay with half the landing looking on. The wine runs clear and dark and smells of the stone cellar it came from. A lord's steward holds the cup. A priest stands behind him and looks at it.
That is wine. I had forgotten. For six weeks I have been pouring my lord something a Rhine man swore was wine, and my lord has been very patient with me.
He keeps Christmas with forty at his table. Name me a price before somebody from the other bank does.
It is Lent, and wine is all the comfort a fasting house is allowed. Name me a price.
We have said Mass since All Saints with wine I would not offer to a creditor. I do not ask a gift. I only mention it, in your hearing, twice.
Sell the fleet's casks on the quay today
Sell half, and take the steward's order for more at his price
Give one cask to the church for the Mass, and sell the rest

By evening the fleet's casks are gone and wine is a little cheaper on this quay than it was at dawn. Your part is a hundred and eighty pennies. The casks under your own thwarts are still yours to sell.
Half goes on the quay, a hundred and ten pennies to you. For the rest the steward cuts a tally: three casks of Seine wine within a hundred and twenty days, at half as much again as the quay pays.

One cask is rolled up to the church door, and the priest walks beside it the whole way with his hand on the staves. The rest sells the better for it: a hundred and fifty pennies to you. Your name is said at the altar on Sunday, with the saint's.
The first cup
The first cask is broached on the quay with half the landing looking on. The steward tastes. He holds it in his mouth for a moment, looking at you, and then looks about for somewhere to spit.
I have a crock of herrings at home that would thank you for this. My lord would not.
Look at the staves. Started, here and here. Somebody drove a bung on working wine. It let the air in to get its own back.
And thick as a ditch. This has been rolled about like a drunk at a wedding and never filled after.
I will take it. Not as wine. Fish do not mind. Forty-five pennies for the lot, and you tell nobody I paid so much.
Call it vinegar and sell it to the salter as vinegar
Mend it with honey and pepper and sell it up the coast as spiced wine
Pour a cup for anyone who asks, and say whose hand was on the bung
Forty-five pennies. The salter's boys roll it away. It is honest vinegar, sold as vinegar, and there is nothing more to be said for it.

Ten pennies of honey and a pinch of pepper, by an old Roman rule. Three landings up the coast, where nobody saw the steward's face, it sells as spiced wine for a hundred and forty. It is even quite good, warm.
Honey and pepper, by an old Roman rule. The first buyer is the steward's cousin. You get twenty pennies from a man who wants it for his horses, and the steward gets the story.

You pour for whoever asks and say plainly what was done to it and who did it. People pay a little out of kindness, thirty pennies in all, and for the cask wood. The steward says he will buy from you next year, to see whether a man learns.
The two halves of the tally
Radbern's house, on the second dam. Aldburg clears the table, lays her half of the hazel stick on it with the notches up, and waits for yours.
The steersman came in two days ago. My father died at Martinmas. They put him in the monks' ground, in a plaster box that others have lain in before him. He would have asked what they charged.
I am told you fetched my water for nine nights. I do not remember it. Aldburg says that is no reason not to believe it.
They say on the dams that the wine kept. So there is something to reckon.
They say on the dams that the wine turned. Then we reckon what there is. A tally is for bad years too. Mostly for bad years.
The steersman says our best casks went along the strand to an Englishman, with my father on the straw. I would like to hear what they fetched. From you.
Your half.
Lay your half beside hers, and every cask and penny with it
Count the Englishman's two hundred and forty pennies onto her table
Give her a short reckoning: casks leak, and the dead keep no tally

The two halves close like a mouth. She counts the notches with her thumbnail, twice, and then counts out your part: a hundred and twenty pennies. She says it is the first year the stick has come home the same length as it went.

You count it out in twelves. She watches every one. When the last is down she pushes a hundred back across the table for your part, and says an Englishman's silver is as good as wine, and keeps better.
You tell her that casks leak. She says her father always said so. She does not ask to see your half of the stick. When you have gone she sits a long while with hers, counting notches.
The next October

Saint Denis's Mass again: the same bells, the same strand, the same mud. This year three people want your boat. Radbern's ship lies by the willows, the cellarer is coming down the path from the gate, and the Englishman is already waving.
I came up with the ship myself. The house needs a small boat that can turn, and a master who brings a stick home whole. I know of one.
I counted the notches. I say nothing more on the saint's day. There is room on this strand for both of us, a good way apart.

The lord abbot has casks for a city over the sea, and a letter for the king's reeve there. He says the saint was once promised a landing place on that strand, and that promises to saints do not die with kings. He wants a boat that can turn, and a master who can be quiet.
I heard about last year's cargo. Everyone spoils one. The lord abbot says a man who has spoiled one is safer than a man who has not yet.

Or do it my way. Your silver and mine in one purse, no old man's stick, no monk's letter. I have found a cellar at Rotomagus with a door on the strand. Buy here, lay it down there, and sell it when we like and not when the weather likes.
Sail with Radbern's house again
Take the abbot's casks and his letter over the sea to Lundenwic
Buy for yourself this year, with the Englishman's silver beside yours
Aldburg splits a new stick. The buying takes a fortnight. She says there will be something to say when the fair closes, and that you should be on the strand to hear it.

Two casks with the abbey's mark, and a letter sewn in oiled linen that you are to give into the reeve's own hand on the Strand at Lundenwic, before Lent if the sea allows. The cellarer blesses the boat. He has not done that before.
You buy beside Leofstan, cask for cask, and argue over every one. Aldburg watches from the willows and does not come over. He will wait for you at Rotomagus on the way down, he says, with the key.
Hands on the strand
The fair is closing. The stalls are coming down, the strand is half empty, and the casks are stowed in the ship and in your boat. Radbern's house offers you its hand before the other shipmen.
Twenty-two Octobers. I am too old for a twenty-third at the steering oar. Aldburg has the head for it and you have the boat. I will sit in the stern and tell you both what you are doing wrong.
My father lies up there by the church wall. I would like him to hear this, so I will say it loudly.

One reckoning for the ship and the boat. Each bears the other's fire and wreck. No oath: the king does not like merchants swearing to one another, and a hand given before witnesses has always been enough on the dams.
You spoiled a cargo and came and said so. I have known men who never spoiled one and whom I would not trust with a bucket.

The cellarer tells me the Frisians and the English wish to ask me something together. That has not happened before in my time. I am a Lombard: I know what it is to be a stranger at another man's fair. Ask.
Join hands: one reckoning, two boats, no oath
Join hands, and go with the English to ask the abbot for a strand of your own
Take your share in silver and stay your own man

Hands are joined on the strand before nine shipmen and the abbey's toll man, who was passing. Your part of two Octobers comes to nine hundred pennies. From now on the ship and the boat keep one tally, and you know the river from the sea to the saint as well as any Frisian living.

Hands are joined; then Frisians and English go up to the gate together, which the porter has never seen. The abbot hears them out. He has it written: the strand from the willows to the island is for the men from over the sea while the fair lasts, a plot above it for their casks, and the toll taken by the keel, once, and not by the cask. Fifteen hundred pennies is your part of the two years. It is the first time the merchants of this fair have had anything of the saint's in writing.

You thank her and take silver: eleven hundred pennies for two Octobers. She says the offer does not spoil, unlike some things. The boats go down the river together, as Frisian boats have every autumn since anyone's grandfather, and part at the sea.
The saint's landing place

On the Strand at Lundenwic the king's reeve has the abbot's letter read to him twice by a clerk of Saint Paul's. He holds a cup of the abbot's wine while he listens, and by the second reading it is empty.

The abbot greets the reeve. He says that the late king, of good memory, promised Saint Denis a landing place in this port, and that he trusts the promise is remembered here as it is there. He sends wine. He names the bearer as a man to be believed.
The late king promised a great many things to a great many saints, and told me about none of them. I witness every sale on this strand. I witnessed no such gift.
It is very good wine. I say so freely. It does not make the letter truer. It makes me more willing to wish that it were.

I can do this much. There is an empty plot above the tide line. If a man I know stands surety for the dues, before witnesses, I can let it to the saint, and the king can make it a gift or not when he hears. I know you. I do not know the abbot.

The abbot's last lines are for the bearer. If there is a landing place, he is to keep it. If there is none, he may ask the abbot's writing for himself at the fair, or take a carrier's wage. The abbot says he is to choose with his head.
Stand surety yourself: the plot for the saint, and you its keeper
Leave the plot to the kings. Ask the abbot's writing for yourself at the fair
Sell the wine, carry the silver back, and take a carrier's wage

Sixty pennies go on ale for the witnesses and a gift the reeve does not look at. Posts are driven above the tide line. From this winter Saint Denis has a landing place at Lundenwic, and it is true because you made it so; you keep it, sell the abbey's wine from it, and take your part, thirteen hundred pennies in the first season. You owe the saint a cask a year for ever, and the abbot can count.

You tell the reeve that plots are for kings to give. He is relieved, and buys the wine. At the next fair the abbot has it written that you trade as Saint Denis's own merchant and pay no toll there. Nine hundred pennies is your part of the wine. The landing place stays a thing the abbey says it was promised.

The wine sells on the Strand in an afternoon. You carry the silver back across the sea, short by nothing, and the cellarer counts out a carrier's wage, six hundred pennies, and shows you a dry corner of the storehouse that is yours to use. He says the lord abbot had hoped for more, and expected this.
A cellar under the wall

At Rotomagus the Englishman unlocks a vaulted cellar under the south wall: old stone, dry, cold, with a door on the strand. Three berths down lies Radbern's ship, and her steersman is watching you both go in.

Roman, the man says, or older. It has kept something cold for five hundred years. It may as well be ours. Wine laid here in November can go over the sea at Candlemas, when the others have none left to sell.
Your boat this side, mine on the Hamwic side, the cellar between. Half and half. I do not swear. I pay.
She counted the notches. She told me to say nothing to you, so I am saying that she told me.
So you go alone. She said you would, sooner or later. She said to wish you a dry cellar, and she meant most of it.
The house has a ship and no master. A woman cannot take her up this river every autumn on a hired steersman's word. If somebody offered silver for the hull, she would have to listen.
Take the cellar with the Englishman, half and half
Buy the dead man's ship from his daughter, at a price she cannot refuse
Take the cellar, and send Aldburg a third of the first winter unasked

The key is cut in two patterns. The first winter's wine, sold at Candlemas over the sea, brings you eight hundred pennies. Radbern's ship still comes up the river in October. Her people do not berth near you, and nobody on the strand asks why.

Four hundred pennies for a sea ship worth several times that. The steersman carries the offer home and carries back her mark. The ship is yours, with the cellar to fill her from. Radbern's house sells its place on the dam before spring. On the strand at the next fair the Frisians make room for you, and no more than room.

You take the cellar, and at Candlemas you send a third of your winter down the coast to the second dam, with no message. Six hundred pennies remain to you. In October her steersman lays the ship alongside your boat on the saint's strand, as if it had always been so.
Radbern's house on the second dam at Dorestat sails with a second keel now, on one tally.
At the fair of Saint-Denis the abbot has given the men from over the sea a strand of their own in writing, and takes his toll there by the keel.
Saint Denis of the Franks has a landing place on the Strand at Lundenwic. A Frisian keeps it and sells the abbey's wine there.
Radbern's daughter has sold her father's ship, and the house's place on the second dam is for sale.

A timber dam head at Dorestat on a late summer evening: a grey-bearded Frisian shipman in a long cloak looks down into a small open boat; behind him a young woman holds a split hazel stick; a broken boat lies hauled out on the bank.

A row of small ships under the grey Roman wall of Rotomagus at slack water in autumn mist: a toll man with a tally and a boy works along them; in one boat a man sits very still with a pilgrim's staff and a large bundle.

The crowded river strand below the long church of Saint-Denis on a bright October morning: boats drawn up side by side, carts of casks, stalls, smoke; in front a tonsured toll man and a Frank in a short cloak each hold out a hand to the same merchant.
Inside a long stone storehouse lit from one door: three rows of casks; a stout monk with keys at his belt bends with his ear to a cask and one finger raised; two merchants wait behind him.

A low hospice room at the abbey gate by rushlight: an old Frisian on straw presses half a hazel stick into a younger man's hand; in the doorway, against the grey day, an Englishman stands with a purse.

Under the wall of Rotomagus on a cold clear day: a wiry cooper kneels in a small boat with his ear near a cask and his knuckle raised to rap it, a mallet and a jug beside him, willow hoops over his shoulder.

A small open boat running under a reefed sail in a steep grey winter sea at dawn: ice on the ropes, three casks lashed amidships, a man crouched over one with a mallet, looking up at the steersman for the word.
A winter quay with a small crowd: a cask on its side with a spigot, dark wine running into a cup; a well-dressed steward drinks with his eyes shut; a priest behind him leans in to look.
The same winter quay and crowd: the steward holds the cup at arm's length with his mouth twisted; a cask with two sprung staves; at the edge a man in a salt-stained apron counts on his fingers.

A Frisian house by the hearth in winter: a bare table, half a notched hazel stick lying on it; a young woman sits with her hands folded, looking up at the merchant in the doorway who holds the other half.

The strand of Saint-Denis again in October sun: the merchant stands by his small boat; from the left a Frisian woman by a ship, from the path a monk with keys, from the right an Englishman with his arm raised, all three looking at him.

The emptying strand at the close of the fair under a low November sky, stalls coming down: a man and a woman clasp hands over a cask head before a half-ring of shipmen; the abbey church stands behind.

The open beach at Lundenwic on a winter afternoon, ships drawn up on the shingle: an English reeve with a silver cup, a young clerk reading from a strip of parchment, the merchant waiting, two casks with a burned mark at their feet.

A low arched door in the foot of the Roman wall of Rotomagus, open on a dark vaulted cellar: an Englishman holds up a key to the merchant; down the strand behind them a steersman on a larger ship watches with folded arms.
